utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I think it was for you to address us on the dossier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. (Interpretation) First of all, I consider it necessary to point out that I have submitted a brief in writing in accordance with your ruling, and the main arguments regarding procedure, on the basis of which we are opposed to the proposal of the Prosecution to enter the Tulica file into evidence as a whole, are contained in that brief. For that reason, I shall not go back to those points so as to avoid repetition. Similarly, Mr. Kordic's Defence has presented the arguments, which we fully ascribe to, and I should just like to add a few points which I feel need to be mentioned. My learned friend, the Prosecutor, at the beginning of his statement, informed us that he was disappointed by the fact that the Defence does not wish to assist the Prosecutor in presenting the case. I must say that that is a totally irrelevant argument. Obviously, it is not the job of the Defence to assist the Prosecution in presenting its case. We are two opposing parties and our interests differ. Secondly, that argument reminds me of another one. It would be rather like if the Defence were to object that the Prosecutor did not consult the Defence when it was amending the indictment at a time when the Defence had already been identified and was actively involved in the case. All I wish to say is that this is a completely erroneous approach and, hence, perhaps some of the reasons for such an approach. I think that the key issue here is not what the Defence wants. The key issue is whether the Rules of Procedure and Evidence prescribe or permit a certain method of production of evidence. Of course, the answer is that the Rules regulate, in some detail, the method of the production of evidence, and also we have certain sources of law, in practice and in theory, and also case law within other jurisdictions, and I am referring to both systems, the civil law and the common law system. Therefore, in my submission, the Court should determine, after this extended debate on the subject, primarily on the basis of the provisions contained in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence combined with a necessary degree of recourse to other case law which the Court deems justified. I think that during the debate, it has been stated innumerable times that the Rules of this Tribunal and international law, in general, without any doubt, protect the right of the Defence to cross-examination of each and every witness and the right of the Defence to critically examine any other produced kind of evidence. So far, the practice of the Tribunal shows that the kind of procedure being suggested by the Prosecution has no where been accepted. In the course of the discussion, the Defence has submitted, and the Prosecution also in its first submission, the way in which ex-Yugoslav law regulated examination of witnesses. I should like to summarise those procedures as follows: In the Law on Criminal Procedure in the former Yugoslavia and the present-day states that have emanated from that system have more or less taken over the same regulations or made only minor amendments to them. The general principle was that the witness must always testify directly in court. Let me not go into the principles on which this rule is based, but it was always a rule that the Trial Chamber has to see that witness because of the principle on direct examination and because the Court must be able to form its own impression about every witness. Reading of witness statements in court in the former Yugoslavia and in the newly formed states was a rare exception, and without, again, going into any details, even when those statements were read, the statement that would be read would be the one that he made before the court investigator, so this is a judicial body and not an investigative body, so the statement is read in the form envisaged by the Law on Criminal Procedure and a statement given under oath. According to the practice established in our courts, statements could not be read under any other circumstances, nor could anyone testify about a witness who told him something. Let me repeat once again, though this has also been mentioned, the Prosecution is offering here a court investigator as a substitute for the witness, and the investigator is described as a court investigator, though that is not correct because he is the Prosecution investigator, so by definition, he is attached to one party in the proceedings and, by definition, he cannot be an unbiased and independent authority. I should like, furthermore, to draw attention to a practical problem that we may be confronted with if we were to accept the Prosecutor's proposition, that instead of examining the witness, we hear the investigator and even documents be tendered through that investigator; namely, we would, without any doubt, come across the problem of equality of arms or the equality of parties and the means at their disposal. What do I mean? The Prosecution has used for its investigations its investigators' division, and we know from this case and from others, the team of prosecutors, that is, our colleagues on the opposite side, did not speak to the witnesses, or if they did, they did so on the basis of the statements provided by the investigators. Contrary to that, the Defence and the attorneys representing the accused here also acted as investigators. In our specific case, the Cerkez Defence does have an investigator as a member of the team who has examined a certain number of witnesses, but let me mention that I personally have interviewed far more witnesses than my investigator. Let me not dwell on the implications because the picture would be a caricature, because if the Prosecutor calls the investigator who is expected to recount what the witness told him, then, because of the equality of parties in the proceedings, perhaps we could find ourselves in the position that I should be called as a witness to tell Your Honours what I did as an investigator. Whether my colleague would then cross-examine me, I don't know, but in any event, this would be absurd, or at least we would not have equality of parties or equality of arms for both parties. If the Rules had envisaged any opportunity which we could have reasonably identified in the course of the preparations and if the Defence could have concluded from them that, in the course of the preparations, the Defence should have had independent investigators, we either were not able to read the Rules or we didn't have enough foresight, but, in any event, this never occurred to the Defence. There is no denying that the burden of proof lies with the Prosecutor. It is the Prosecution that has issued the indictment and defined it; it is the Prosecution that has to produce the evidence if he has it. If he doesn't have the evidence, then there is no case. That is put in very simple terms. We are all in justice long enough to have witnessed cases when there was no case and other cases which had a case, thanks to the evidence, but it is impossible to claim that there is a major case and no evidence. Therefore, the evidence that the Prosecutor has must be presented here in court, and the Court, the Trial Chamber, must be able to see those witnesses. Only then, that will be in accordance with the general principles of international criminal law and, of course, the Rules of this Tribunal. The Prosecutor has that responsibility, and he must acquit himself of that responsibility. In this way, offering dossiers and the mediation of the investigator, in actual fact, the burden of proof is being shifted to the Defence but also to the Trial Chamber, and that clearly is not the task of the Defence or the Trial Chamber. Secondly, in this way, the OTP is actually suggesting that, despite the Rules, lower standards be applied in the production of evidence than those applied in all civilised systems, both civil law and common law systems. In our deep conviction, this International Tribunal should serve as a model court which will and should contribute to establishing higher standards in criminal proceedings rather than opening the possibility for the application of lower standards than those existing in other courts. The Prosecution has mentioned here the principle of a fair trial and the right to a fair trial, as well as the principle of economy or efficiency of the proceedings. It is our belief that, combined with other principles that are applied in the proceedings, those principles have priority. I think there is no need to argue that the principle of a fair trial certainly has precedence over expeditiousness. We are all at times frustrated by the complications and waste of time in the course of the proceedings, but that does not mean to say that we have the right to violate the principle of a fair trial for the parties, not only for the accused but also for the parties and for the Trial Chamber. All in all, I think that the Prosecutor should have had all this in mind in the course of the investigation and when he issued the indictment, and especially when the indictment was amended, because we now find ourselves in a situation when an attempt is being made to remedy something that was not done when it should have been done. Once again, and if I may, I should like to underline the question of stipulation. This is a tested mechanism, regardless of differences that do exist from one country to another, but basically all of us jurists understand one another, regardless of the systems we come from. We know what stipulations are; the establishment of undisputed facts by both parties. I must say that stipulations in this case were of a minimum degree. Maybe they are not even worth mentioning, but not because of the Defence and the lack of cooperation on the part of the Defence but because the Defence, when certain points were proposed for stipulation, the Defence could not reasonably take a position, except on a few peripheral matters, because the process of discovery had not been completed. It is not possible to expect the Defence to be cooperative with respect to stipulations if, at that point in time, the Defence does not have all the materials at its disposal. I must recall something that I said when we started the discussion about the Tulica dossier. I myself made some proposals when the Prosecutor made their second appeal for the admission of facts. I admitted some, I rejected others, but I myself proposed certain changes so that we could then discuss those revised definitions, but I never received an answer. Let me just say a word or two about the reports as a part of the Tulica dossier. Please do not misunderstand me, but I should like to use an example that we had recently to avoid excessive theorising and in order to be more practical. We had the McLeod report, which was a highly interesting one, but I cannot but note that Witness McLeod is certainly a far more qualified person than the average OTP investigator. There can be no doubt about that. Nonetheless, only one document that was in the report which you saw was this list of prestigious Muslims. I think there was 16 or 13 names on that list, and it was stated that all those individuals were interned already on the 16th of April, and this was used in the context of trying to prove an allegation which I'm not going to go back to. But our analysis has shown that two out of those 13 persons were never detained, and they had told this Tribunal that two days prior to McLeod, two were dead by the 16th of April and four were detained three or five days later than alleged in this report. Therefore, the report, as a document compiled by a qualified person, certainly a more qualified one than the investigators we have here, had a number of errors in it, and now we're expected to accept the tendering of reports compiled by various investigators, various employees, and to accept them without challenging them. I think that would really be quite contrary to some fundamental principles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, when you refer to reports in that connection, are you referring to the on-site investigation reports by the Sarajevo Court and the forensic experts?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No, not for these, because I accepted these reports, with some minor exceptions, but because they were compiled in accordance with the procedural law of the country I come from, which I believe provides sufficient guarantees, because they were not produced by investigating organs, they were simply one of the procedures that are part of the investigating procedure, and I did not see any major problems there. It is up to us to accept them or not to accept them as undisputed. However, there are other kinds of reports here which are not acceptable. But even the ones you mentioned, let me give you an example, there is a record of an investigation by an investigating judge. In the original, the title is, "Investigating Judge's On-site Report." There is a document attached to this report at page R00600048. In this document, the forensic technician, who drew up some of the material which is enclosed, inserted a subtitle, "The examination of ten people killed by the HVO." This is a quotation, but this cannot be accepted, because when an investigating judge conducts an on-site investigation and he has forensic technicians working for him, their job is simply to establish the traces and the facts. However, this forensic technician, who was only supposed to sketch where things were found, put in his own conclusion, because he concluded that these people had been killed by the HVO. It was not his job to conclude this. It's not something that he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I think that is an area where having professional judges is useful, because clearly that's a matter which is or may be in dispute. It's not a matter which that particular expert or investigator could know anything about. He would be merely reporting what he had heard from somebody else, and we would ignore that as evidence. What we would be likely to admit, if we were to admit it, was the matters on which he was supposed to report and on which he did report, those matters which you described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, suppose the Prosecutor sought to adduce the witness statements in the form of affidavit evidence in accordance with Rule 94 ter. Now, what would your reaction be to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) My reaction to the introduction of testimonies made under oath in other cases before this Tribunal is far more flexible, because, first of all, I believe that the Rules provide a mechanism which can ensure this. Secondly, there is already some experience in this regard, and I think that there are several ways of solving this. In my personal opinion, the best way, but it's not the only way, would be to apply Rule, I believe, 89(C) as documentary evidence and possibly to establish whether there is an area in the testimony where the witness was not cross-examined, regardless of which of the parties is involved, whether it's the Defence and the party was not cross-examined by the Prosecution, or whether it's a Prosecution witness who was perhaps not cross-examined in sufficient depth by the Defence counsel because the Defence strategy was different. But there are ways in which we could solve this problem, and I think there are at least two ways in which this can be done. As I have already said, my personal opinion is that 89(C) would be the best way to deal with this. I would like to conclude now, unless you have any further questions, of course. I would just like to remind you, Mr. President, that during this discussion, you mentioned certain things on two occasions, referring to the right to cross-examination. On the 28th day of the trial, on page 125 of the daily count, in lines 23 to 25, you said to my colleague, the Prosecutor -- I think I better read it in English, to avoid conclusion. (In English) "But it is not the Defence who are calling those witnesses, and the Defence are entitled to cross-examine. It is the Prosecution calling the witnesses, and it may be the Prosecution should review its position." (Interpretation) The second time there was a similar discussion on second hearsay, that was on the 11th of May, on page 2232, lines 13 to 15, where you repeated what you had said before. (In English) "Somehow different rules should apply, because this is a difficult case to prove." (Interpretation) I would like to conclude by saying that this is a difficult case. I think we are all aware of the fact that it's a difficult case. But this cannot change the fact that the burden of proof is on the Prosecution and that the Prosecutor has to produce evidence before this Court, whether it's material evidence or witnesses. If he's unable to do so, with all the theoretical cooperation of the Defence and all the goodwill of the Tribunal, there will not be a case. That is all I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I distribute skeletons of my reply and take you quickly through it. The position now is clear that the Defence are saying that each and every element of the crime must be proved by evidence from the witness box, and since, of course, we only intend to call relevant evidence and not to bother, save to the most limited degree, the background material, that means that every bit of evidence has got to come from there. It was interesting to note that Mr. Smith stopped short to saying that each and every exhibit has to be proved in the same complete method, because I think they recognise that that would really bring absurdity to these proceedings and, of course, because they appreciate they have been allowed, by our attitude and the Court's practice, a very permissive approach in relation to exhibits on all sides. Their argument is, in reality, a straightforward common-law argument to the effect that hearsay is inadmissible, and it's interesting to see to what it would lead if it's right. First, there is no difference in category between hearsay in the form of written statements and hearsay in any other form that this Tribunal regularly admits. If this argument is right, that is, the Defence position is correct, it would lead inevitably to further criticism of the admission of hearsay generally. Presumably, the argument should be that that evidence is all totally inadmissible, for it could be argued that each and every witness, using the word "witness" in a general sense, whose testimony, used in a general sense, is given second-hand as hearsay, should be before the Tribunal for cross-examination. But, second, and this is the matter least to have in mind, if the Defence counsel's argument is correct, then putting ourselves in the position of Defence counsel in all cases, they would be not only permitted but, in reality, obliged to admit nothing of any significance in any case and to require all evidence to be proved by live witnesses, with obvious consequences for this Tribunal and the length of its trials. Our argument is, of course, that the witness for whom there are rights to cross-examine is the person who comes to the witness box, who produces statements, written or verbal, in the same way as he does or she does with other evidence, exclusion of that material being within the Tribunal's discretion. It's only right that I should draw to your attention that there is a different formulation, apparently favoured by the European Court of Human Rights, for the term "witness," namely that "witness" should refer to any person whose statements are placed before the court and are taken into account by it, and you can find that referred to in the Kostovski case, in the extract from the textbook provided and to which I will make further reference shortly. That alternative formulation favoured by the ECHR is in a setting where its own authorities recognises that the right to cross-examine such witnesses is not absolute. It may be that the formulation I've proposed where the word "witness" does relate to the person who comes to give evidence, and the other material should be differently described, whether it's the gun, the dagger, or the written statement of someone else, is the more logical and, in a sense, the purer, although the second formulation may seem more reflective of the ordinary use of language. In any event, there may be no practical difference in outcome between these two formulations of the definition for the word "witness," there always being a discretion to admit or reject evidence if it does not come live from the witness box, even if relevant. It's worth noting that Rule 89(C), upon which Mr. Kovacic would rely, permits the admission of any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value, and that, of course, requires that hearsay statements that are being admitted regularly by this Chamber and others rank as evidence, that that accordingly fits with the first formulation, the one that I have proposed. I note, however, that affidavits, perhaps not unsurprisingly, are in the formulation of 94 ter, the affidavits of witnesses. I turn from those general observations to a few observations on the law from England and Wales to which we were referred initially by Judge Robinson, and I'm sorry that I wasn't able immediately, he raised the case of Radak, to deal with it, not then being aware of it. Sections 23 and 26 of the 1988 Act which were permissive of the adduction of written statements in certain circumstances are collectively to impose a presumption against such admissibility in the absence of leave of the court based on the interests of justice, and that, of course, broadly speaking, reflects the approach we are taking. We are not asking for wholesale admission of material or anything of the like. We are simply seeking to identify what it is appropriate should and what it is wholly inappropriate should be brought all the way here from the former Yugoslavia. As the Court may know, in the test for Sections 23 and 26 in the English law, there's the high standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt that falls on the Prosecution when they seek to satisfy the terms of the section, although a lower, more generous standard is made appropriate for the Defence. If the Court has before it the extract from the textbook Archbold that I provided, using page numbers rather than the paragraph numbers which are sometimes less easy to find, page number 1121, the third sheet, the third sheet and at the foot of page 1121, the following passage appears: "Where a judge admitted the statement of a witness on the ground that he would not give oral evidence through fear, there was no violation of the accused's rights under the European Convention on Human Rights, although Article 6(3)(d) conferred on anyone charged with a criminal offence the right to examine or have examined witnesses against him as one of his minimum rights. This was merely an aspect of the right to a fair trial guaranteed by Article 6(1), and since the judge had satisfied himself in accordance with Section 26 of the 1988 Act that it was in the interests of justice to admit the statement, having taken into account, in particular, any risk of unfairness to the accused, the trial considered as a whole had been fair." That's the case of Thomas and Flannagan. Radak, which I discover is in the supplement to the latest volume of Archbold, turned, as Mr. Smith correctly analysed, on a shortcoming of the prosecution and not specifically on a breach of the convention. The transcript, which I trust you have before you, repays some careful attention. Again, I will refer, having dealt with a detail in Section 26 from the skeleton, to the transcript by page numbers. First, Section 26(b)(ii), and I give the photocopy reference, in identifying the discretion factors that the judge has to take into consideration before he can admit such a statement, refers to: "Any risk, having regard in particular to whether it is likely to be possible to controvert the statement of the person if the person making it does not attend to give oral evidence in the proceedings, that its admission will result in unfairness ..." So the important phrase is "likely to be possible to controvert." Now, in the transcript of Radak at page 9, line 8, the Court of Appeal made these observations dealing with the particular facts of that case which all hinged on the single statement of the single witness, but at line 8, the court said this by way of definition of "controvert": "A defendant might controvert the statement by giving evidence or calling the evidence of other witnesses, but might also do so by cross-examination of or putting Mr. Shifrin's credibility in issue. It was accepted by the prosecution that none of the defendants was in a position by calling evidence to controvert Mr. Shifrin's evidence if it were to be read." And they weren't going to be able to controvert it by calling other evidence. This, I think, happily, is the same point I was making when first asked about this case by Judge Robinson some days ago, but for the material we are suggesting can properly be read, it is entirely open if there is a real issue to the Defence to call evidence to the contrary effect. As I said on the first hearing of this particular stage of the argument, of course, if it was known by them in advance that they were in a position so to controvert the statement of a witness, it might be thought to be their duty to raise a good argument why the witness should come to court to be cross-examined, and no doubt, if they had a good argument, he would be here. Similarly, no doubt, if they kept that part of their powder dry and simply called evidence in their case, it might be open to the Prosecution to deal with the matter thereafter by rebuttal. But what is important is that the interpretation of "controvert" is not restricted to cross-examination but includes specifically the calling of other evidence or, indeed, the putting into issue the man's credibility by argument, for example. The same transcript at the foot of the page on the last four lines says this: "Mr. Shifrin's evidence was an essential link in the prosecution's case. It was not merely a formal part of their case. The fact that the defendants have little or no evidence to controvert Mr. Shifrin's statement, in our view, reinforces the submission made on their behalf that it would be unfair if they did not have the opportunity to test the evidence by cross-examination. You cannot conduct an argument with nor ask questions of a piece of paper." If you turn over, please, to page 10 and the penultimate paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On that last point, that it was not merely a formal part of their case, the evidence that the Prosecution would be seeking to adduce in this case would not be merely a formal part of the Prosecution's case, would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I entirely accept that it's not a merely formal part whatever, with deference to the Court of Appeal, a merely formal part of evidence may be. As I said earlier, no evidence is really called unless it is part of the overall chain of evidence that goes to make a conviction appropriate. Very rarely is one allowed the time of the court simply to deal with background material. There is a difference -- well, what does "formal" mean? I'm not sure what they think it meant in that case, but I come later in my skeleton argument to some examples of what might -- one example in particular, to an example of what might be thought to be formal material in, for example, a case of domestic murder, and yet that's the sort of material that can typically be dealt with by being read or admitted in other jurisdictions, and there's no reason why that practice shouldn't happen here. There is, as I know, in the ICTR a case that's proceeded entirely on the basis that the genocide is entirely conceded, and the only issue before the Tribunal is whether the responsibility of the defendant is established. There is no absolute rule that because something is an element, a vital element in the proof of the crime charged against the defendant, that neither he, nor those on his part, can admit it or deal with it shortly. They can. If there is no reason to doubt the accuracy of the material, there is no absolute rule that says that a tribunal has to have the evidence before it live. To some degree, the problem that you raise from that quotation is a problem that turns on its own terms and the use of the word "formal." What is formal? In all cases, some evidence can be described as formal. In all cases, all evidence is probably, in a sense, essential to conviction. If we turn over to page 10, we see that observation, I hope, reflected in the first two lines of the penultimate paragraph where the commission -- I beg your pardon, wherein a quotation from the case of Application against Germany, I think that is, cited in the last line of the previous paragraph, it says this: "The Commission recalls that Article 6(3)(d) of the Convention does not grant the accused an unlimited right to secure the appearance of witnesses in court. Its purpose is rather to ensure equality between the defence and the prosecution as regards the summoning and examining of witnesses ..." If Your Honour's point or if Your Honour's concern is derived from what lies at the foot of the previous page of this judgement, is a concern that wherever there is anything critical, crucial, or whatever it may be, to a conviction, that it has to come live from the witness box, then that passage simply couldn't exist, and yet it does. Can I, before we turn from the assistance, if it is, from the law of England and Wales, to take you on in the extract from the textbook Archbold, first of all, to what you can find at the foot of page 1143. I know I have referred to this passage on an earlier occasion, and I think on the earlier occasion, I mentioned that it was a piece of new legislation thought by some to have been legislation in error, but nevertheless, this is the present position in England and Wales, and at the foot of 1143, paragraph 10-41, Section 68 of the 1996 Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act is set out as giving effect, wide reaching, and I turn over, in that they make any statement falling within Section 5(B) of the Magistrates Court Act, and any deposition taken under Section 97(A) of that act admissible at trial. This is subject to objection by the defence, but any such objection may be overridden by the judge in the interests of justice. As the commentators from Archbold go on to make clear, this provision goes further than any previous legislation on the admissibility of witness statements and depositions. First, there is no restriction of admissibility to cases where the witness is dead, too sick to attend court, or too frightened to give evidence, and it sets out the earlier provisions. Secondly, there is no restriction on the discretion of the judge and no indication as to what factors he should consider. Thirdly, the presumption seems to be in favour of admission of such evidence with the onus being on the defence to object. This is confirmed by Rule 22 of the Crown Court Rules. Next paragraph. It should be borne in mind that under the new regime introduced by the 1996 act, the old system, whereunder a magistrate's court committing an accused for trial would make a series of witness orders full or conditional, in respect of witnesses, has been abolished, and therefore, the provisions of this schedule are not confined to the statements or depositions of non-contentious witnesses, the subject of conditional witness orders. It appears, however, the commentators go on to say that the introduction of such a draconian system was not what was intended. These provisions were introduced at a late stage in the life of the bill in the House of Commons, and upon the House of Lords' subsequent consideration of the Commons amendment, the apparent defects were pointed out that the government was unwilling to accept any amendment, Baroness Blatch saying: "If the evidence ... has been admitted in earlier committal hearings and is not disputed by any parties at the trial, it would be both unnecessary and wasteful to require the presence of witnesses to give that evidence again orally." That is a practice which already exists, and we're not seeking to introduce anything new or revolutionary. As to the discretion to override a Defence objection, Baroness Blatch said that it was anticipated that the courts would turn for guidance to Section 26 of the 1988 Act, which we've already considered. These concessions leave the position extremely vague. In particular, despite Baroness Blatch giving, as examples, a witness who has died or moved abroad, there are no such conditions of admissibility in the Act and it would be quite impossible to read them into it merely on the basis of examples given by the Minister. Secondly, there remains the issue of the burden of proof. Under the Criminal Justice Act, 1925, Section 13, the Prosecutor had to establish the existence of one of the conditions of admissibility to the criminal standard, and under the Criminal Justice Act, 1988, not only is this the case, but also under Section 26, the presumption is against admissibility, so it remains to be seen how much the courts are prepared to read into an Act, something which is plainly not intended to say. Nevertheless, if there is help from the jurisprudence of England and Wales, it is quite clear that the principle of admissibility of written statements is intact and, however the precise words of the latest Act of Parliament may be interpreted, that it is the Court that is going to be exercising decision-making powers, within a properly-exercised discretion, as to which witnesses should attend. Finally, because it has created some concern, I think, amongst the defendants, I've made available to you, to be handed up, please, and it's on the bench in front of you, the one sheet, and this deals with the suggestion that any requirement for defendants to make their case plain is to place a burden on them that is inappropriate. In England and Wales, by Sections 5 and 6 of the same 1996 Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act, there is now compulsory disclosure by the accused under Section 5 where the Act applies, which is to trial on indictments where the Prosecutor has complied with the duty of disclosure, and if one casts one's eyes down to subparagraph 6, there is the requirement, or subparagraphs 5 and 6, there are the requirements that the accused must give a defence statement to the court and the prosecutor setting out, in general terms, the nature of the accused's defence, indicating the matters on which he takes issue with the prosecution, and setting out, in the case of each such matter, the reason why he takes issue, so that in the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom, there are developments that reflect, it may be thought, the efficiencies that we seek and, indeed, the method by which we say they can be accomplished. If I can just turn then now to the civil system, in the civil system statements other than those taken by an investigating judge are admissible, and if the Court has in mind or has access to the extract from the book of Stefanus Stavros, there are passages at page 231 and the footnote at 232 of some assistance. At 231, the author, in the middle of the page and in reviewing or partway through the process of reviewing authorities, says this: "It soon became apparent that untested hearsay evidence could not be excluded altogether. Many States' parties allow, to one degree or another, for their admission in criminal proceedings. This is particularly true of continental inquisitorial systems where the case file forms part of the evidence before the court. This is compiled at the preindictment stage by an investigating judge, whose conclusions usually carry weight with the court and often contain statements of witnesses who do not appear at the trial hearing. "Rather valid reasons are sometimes adduced for the failure of such witnesses to testify. Parliamentary and family privilege, as well as the limitations involved in the special procedures for the examination of persons highly placed in the State, have been accepted by the convention organs as compatible, in principle, with Article 6." We turn over the page to the footnote number 734, which is given on the fourth line of the text: "Under the general proposition, equality of arms has been respected --" well, it's quoting the Unterpertinger case, in which no violation was found, and I start at the top of the page. "As the exclusion of witnesses operated for both the Defence and the Prosecution, equality of arms had been respected. Article 6(1) had not been violated, as the total lack of direct evidence in the case was remedied by the existence of other circumstantial evidence which the domestic court had considered sufficient to warrant the applicant's conviction." Then the footnote itself identifies the circumstantial evidence which comprised the statements made by relatives to the police, the police report summarising and commenting on them, medical reports on the injuries of the victims, the divorce file between the applicant and the wife, and, finally, the applicant's own defence arguments and the personal impression he made upon the Court and so on. So, as we've advanced before, all sorts of material, and as I think is well known in various civil systems, are admissible. I go on to say this: The right to dispute every element of a case, which is, I think, a recognised right, is not a right to cross-examine every possible witness in all circumstances. There is a right to a fair trial, and if the trial is fair without cross-examination, there is no breach of the European Convention. A case in support of that, which we have in French at the moment but not in English, is Doorson, and I can make that available to the Chamber, if it would help. If it's possible to dispute a statement, for example, by showing conflicts, exactly as the Defence have been doing, exactly as my friend Mr. Kovacic was making clear today when he was, for example, commenting on McLeod, if it's possible to show conflicts in that way, then you can devalue the evidence to the Trial Judge or, alternatively, you can justify the calling of the material witness for cross-examination. That accomplishes a fair trial. There is no, as we've seen, absolute right to have every declarant, as Mr. Smith would call them, every percipient observer, present for the purposes of cross-examination. It's interesting to note that in the Kostovski case, both the witnesses were anonymous. They gave crucial and decisive evidence against the accused. Because they were anonymous, they were available for questioning only via an examining magistrate. I think questions had to be submitted to the magistrate, and he asked them of the anonymous witnesses, spoken to out of the presence of the lawyers, as I understand it. In these circumstances, the anonymity affected the ability of the parties to question the witness, and it may be, fundamentally, to dispute the material at all. This is not a question simply of not being able to cross-examine. These European cases do not bar the use of statements of the sort we seek to use. In any event, there is no question of wholesale use, as categorised by Mr. Smith, and it has never been our intention to rely on written statements, as a matter of course, for direct evidence concerning the accused, unless, of course, such material was agreed. Of course, that material which directly implicates the accused, we would expect and would have to come here. In all cases cited by us from Stavros' book, the questioned evidence was critical in a way entirely different from the way in which the accounts of the villagers would be relevant here. Of course, their collective accounts may be essential for conviction, because their accounts show the commission of on-the-ground crimes that are charged against the defendants. Then to return to Judge Robinson's point that he earlier raised with me, in a murder case, the pronouncement of death by a doctor or the account by the pathologist of the mechanism of death is a crucial element of the case, and yet all too regularly it's material that is adduced unchallenged, because the issue is not how it was done but who was responsible. In short, the European cases do not allow for a fishing expedition by the Defence and are decisions given in cases where the proper joining of issues had been established. It may be worth noting what Stavros said on the Asch case, because he observes or suggests that in that case, where the conviction or a finding of the lower court was upheld, he notes that the European Court appeared to have reservations concerning the good faith of the applicant who, in the course of the national proceedings, had not made any serious attempts to dispute the complainant's version of events. Here, we propose that witnesses would be available for cross-examination wherever the Court is persuaded, in good faith, that there is a serious dispute. We've never suggested otherwise. We say that is preferable to what may have been raised as a possibility by Judge Robinson and possibly by Judge Bennouna, namely, that there should be, as it were, witnesses brought in by the plane load to say, "That's my statement and it's right," and then to be subject to no significant or helpful questioning. I think the following point, paragraph 14, has already been picked up by a member of the Court, but Rule 94 of our own Rules, which allows cross-examination of affidavit witnesses, does so only where the party objects and, and the "and" is emphasised in my text, not in the original of course, and the Trial Chamber so rules. That Rule thus recognises, in relation to a category of evidence, the power to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You are now coming to the gist of the subject, or we're rather turning around the same subject without making much progress, because reference to all these cases, national and European, I don't think that that is helping us much, because after all, we are an International Tribunal here which does not always have behind it the cooperation of States, as is the case in the European tribunal that you are referring to. Even the case that you have just cited, the Radak case, it was stated that: (In English) "Witnesses residing abroad whose presence at the trial cannot be enforced by the trial court are examined on commission by a court at their place of residence." (Interpretation) This means we keep coming back to the question that has been put to you, and that is the following: The investigators are a part of the Office of the Prosecutor, and we are not in a national framework where we have court investigators which may sometimes be independent of the prosecution, as is the case in many countries. We're dealing with the situation in which the Prosecutor has several functions; policing, investigator, investigating judge, and so on. So we're asking you, in order to have these documents admitted and these statements, they have to be covered by some other authority and not just yours. That is the basic question. That is the gist of the matter. So when you're talking about affidavits here, there is a statement under oath, and the question has been put to you, I think, by my colleague Judge Robinson, either you're going through a statement under oath, in which case the witness is committed and his own credibility is involved under penalty of sanctions, or you have national authority to rely on. What I'm saying applies equally to the Defence, because the Defence may also be confronted with such problems, and it may be confronted with certain obstructions on the part of States, and it may have difficulty in bringing witnesses because of that. So we have two elements. First, we're in an International Tribunal here which has not the authority to impose itself but needs the support of others, which is not always provided. So if you wish to remedy this, you can either have a statement under oath, as has been said, or affidavits, or, as I think Mr. Kovacic said, he recognised himself certain inquiries carried out by local judges, death certificates provided by local authorities. So we could go through another passage and not just through the Prosecutor, because the Defence tells you that the Prosecutor's channel is not sufficient because it would call in question the equality of arms, bearing in mind that that principle is not the same applied in a national court and in an International Tribunal such as ours. This was stated in the Tadic case. So I think if you can help us along those lines, then, I think, we can make greater progress. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've dealt, of course, with the authorities, European and United Kingdom, out of respect of the argument of my friends opposite and because Judge Robinson raised and I didn't conclusively deal with the matter the first time I was addressing you. As to the position of the investigators and their separateness or not from the Office of the Prosecutor, that is no different from the position in countries elsewhere for what that is value where there is identity between the police and the CPS, or the prosecuting authority, or whoever else it may be for all practical purposes. That is in no sense a barrier to the adoption of statements taken by those investigators. On the contrary, it is exactly by those investigators that the statements are taken. Such statements are usually headed by, or in fact invariably, I think, headed by a caption that goes to the truth of the statement, as are statements here. In other jurisdictions, the statements may be subject to a penal notice, which isn't available to us here because no such provision has yet been made by the Rules. But it's interesting to note, and if I could invite you just to turn over to the next sheet of my argument for the detail, to paragraph 17, that Judge Jorda and Trial Chamber I, when dealing with the statement of the late Midhat Haskic, the witness in respect of whom, we, in due course, will seek to have a statement read because he's dead. When Judge Jorda dealt with that and permitted the statement to be read, he spoke of the statement being sworn, recognising that in the particular circumstances allowed us by the provision of our Rules, the statement was as far as it could go without it being similar on affidavit or otherwise. I also understand, as a matter of fact, there may be no provisions for affidavits formally in the former Yugoslavia, but that's perhaps a detail. I suppose statements can be taken with some additional formality, if necessary. But there is simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) But, Mr. Nice, do not forget that we are not applying here the law of ex-Yugoslavia or of Great Britain, we're applying the Rules of the Tribunal and the Statutes of the Tribunal, which do not envisage, as you have already been told, 94 ter. You should not refer to national legislation which has no affect on the International Tribunal, especially if it runs counter, directly counter, to a provision of the Statute or the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was simply dealing with the reality of the statement-taking powers available to us and the way they have been recognised by another Chamber of this Tribunal and, indeed, recognised in a way that thereafter was followed by the evidence being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But, in fact, the rule-making body had that point in mind, because there is a reference specifically in the Rule to affidavits signed by other witnesses in accordance with the law or procedure of the State in which such affidavits are signed. So if somebody came along and said, "We can't have an affidavit, we don't recognise them," there is a procedure for obtaining statements or declarations. The term is signed by other witnesses in accordance with the law and procedure of the State. Since I am interrupting you, I wonder whether, first of all, I could draw your attention to the clock. I hope we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I've nearly finished, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could finish, and then there's something I want to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. But because I mustn't leave Judge Bennouna's question unanswered, our argument is and remains that material of all kinds, subject to your discretion under Rule 89(C), is admissible. That includes statements howsoever obtained or taken that there is absolutely nothing wrong with those statements being taken by an officer of the Prosecutor, and there would be nothing wrong with statements being taken by an investigator for the Defence. I accept that. There has to be equality. We say that material can be taken by you, and under your powers of controlling the presentation of evidence, you can decide whether it's going to be acceptable to you or whether you're going to say, "No, that witness has to be called." Paragraph 15, again out of respect for the Defence arguments, I observe that in the Yugoslav code, witnesses and experts shall be summoned except for those whose examination in the trial is not required in the judgement of the presiding judge. It's the duty of that judge to see that the subject matter is fully explained and that the truth is found and that everything is eliminated which prolongs but does not serve to clarify. In conclusion, I make these points: There's been little divergence of witness testimony from what is contained in the statements. Some changes or differences are inevitable. They are not necessarily caused by breaking down, as Mr. Stein would wish. The difference may be caused by anxieties not reflecting dishonesty in any way. As a matter of fact, little has emerged from cross-examination by way of a change of testimony. I've dealt with paragraph 17. Our proposal never suggested the wholesale adoption of written statements. The defendants are not being deprived of the right to cross-examine. They are simply being required to justify cross-examining. They are being required to do so to the Chamber because the Rules do not oblige them to cooperate with us in the way we had hoped and in the way that other systems would require. Although Judge Bennouna, I recognise, may be concerned about national jurisdictions, the analogy from other jurisdictions can help to this extent: When you have a regime that requires the Defence to justify their actions, of course the consequence is that cooperation takes place in order to forestall difficulties. It's, as I said on an earlier occasion, enforced but takes the form of real cooperation. The Defence have previously acknowledged that prior testimony could be read. There is no reason to distinguish between the admission of prior testimony of witnesses and the statements of witnesses. The Defence stated in November of 1998, last year, this: "The second point is that the basic rationale for our motion is the possibility that this case could be handled more speedily and more efficiently by using, in this case, evidence, that is to say, transcripts and exhibits already gone through, produced, and delivery in these other cases, on some basis that the two sides and the Court could agree upon and thus not have to repeat historical testimony. Testimony that's critical concerning, say, military necessity, that might be in the Blaskic case, critical to the predicant defences that our defendant and Mr. Cerkez are alleged to have participated, leaving counsel only during the direct and cross to take on new matters. This may not be feasible, and it may be there is a great deal of other evidence in these other cases that would relieve these witnesses from having to come back to The Hague if counsel and the Court find a procedure by which this is possible." As I think I suggested earlier, the Defence position has hardened or, in any event, become more revealed in recent argument to the position that they are now saying everything has to be proved, and as we saw last week, they now refer to a two and a half year trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where do they refer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stein said that last week in argument. That recognises two things, that they cannot object to the prosecution of a confirmed indictment calling its evidence and that their position might lead to that result. Mr. Kovacic made some further points, which I hope most of them I've swept up as I've been going along. As to his concern about him speaking to witnesses himself, well, first of all, it's not yet known in this case whether Defence witness statements will themselves ever be produced. If they are, the reality is that the Defence will not find themselves in a significantly different position from the Prosecution because, of course, as the Court now knows, the summary documents that are provided are provided frequently in dialogue with one of the lawyers, as we know, indeed, from the statement of Dr. Mujezinovic and the other statement of Mr. Ehsan Bajwa. Statements there were taken by a lawyer and an investigator, so that's a commonplace. If it is desired to present evidence without exposing lawyers to the witness box, there are inevitably techniques by which that can be accomplished. We remain of this position: We've done everything we can to abbreviate this case by serving material for admission and by seeking to discover what truly is not in issue. Mr. Kovacic, it has to be said, has been far more cooperative and has made attempts in the past to agree things, but always his agreements have been trumped, to use an analogy, by the blanket denial of everything by the Kordic Defence which meant that, for the time being, his concessions cannot avail us of anything. We've made all those efforts. If there is no way by which matters can be agreed or matters can be read, then we will simply have to call the evidence to the witness box to prove the case, and we've always been prepared to do that. It will be a dreadful expenditure of time, the expense of other persons waiting trial, if witness after witness is subject to nothing effective in the way of cross-examination. It would be a proper disposal of this issue for this Chamber to either require further elucidation from the Defence of their position on the matters we seek to deal with in the way identified, alternatively, on the basis of their present response, to say no good showing has been revealed why this material may not be read. Accordingly, the Prosecution, who have always intended to call one or so witnesses, can carry on and call the limited number of witnesses they do, but we will take the other evidence read into account. That, of course, would be entirely without prejudice to the ability of the Defence to call other witnesses to a contrary effect at a later stage in the trial, it would be entirely without prejudice to the Defence arguing so as to guarantee a fair trial that one witness is inconsistent with another, whatever, but it would save huge amounts of time and be a credit to this institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just help me, if you would, with this: It's an unusual form of application, really, when you think about it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- because, in fact, it's a series of applications to admit different types of evidence. One approach that we could take would be to admit or exclude the entire dossier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we admitted it, then, of course, there would be no need for further argument, at least as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned. If we excluded it, it would then, of course, be open to you to apply for various parts, it may be, to be put into evidence. A third approach is for us to analyse what's in the dossier and go through it item by item, as it were, making it a series of separate applications. If we were against you on admitting the whole dossier, would you invite us to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exactly so, subject to such further argument as the Defence might seek to make in clarification or amplification of their response. It seems to us that wherever the Defence are saying, "This is simply something out of our knowledge," then that is something much more likely properly to be read and dealt with in that way or by the summary of the investigator. Where they identify a real issue and the Chamber judges it to be a real issue, we wouldn't suggest other than that could justify the witnesses being called, which is, as I understand it, if I can complete the answer, which is, as I understand it, what happens at the examining stage of a civil system or, indeed, both stages, and that's what we have sought to provide as a method. Indeed, since I perhaps have interrupted Your Honour now, but can I just remind the Court overall of how this comes about? It comes about because I'd, first of all, set out how I was going to present evidence, going around the municipalities, hoping to discern from cross-examination what was in issue and then to lead material, ever narrowing my witness base, I hoped, that was relevant to particular areas. Before we got very far advanced on that process, the Court expressed its desire to consider the witness list. The Defence then, in the vernacular, had jumped on the bandwagon, and although their first response may have no bearing, and I would ask that it should, indeed, have absolutely no bearing on any decision, sought impertinently to say two witnesses per village without revealing that they had no intention of admitting a thing and would have come back at the end of the trial to said, "You simply haven't proved your case," and from that stage on, we got involved with methods of abbreviating the trial by greater efficiencies, and that led us to say, "Well, first of all, we divided our witnesses up for you between above- and below-the-line witnesses in an attempt to identify those who might not be needed," although, I have to say, if there are no concessions made, it may well be that some of the below-the-line witnesses who we'd formerly thought we might not have to call might now be necessary because we will be missing bits of evidence in relation to particular counts, however economically I call the evidence. I hope not, but it may come about. Then it was that we advanced this as a possibility to you. So that's the history of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, I think there is a misunderstanding with respect to the question put by my colleague, the President, Judge May. The question was the first possibility, and that is to reject the dossier in its totality; the other is to accept it globally. You were asked if the Trial Chamber was not prone to accept it as a whole, would you agree if we could go category by category, not statement by statement, but legal category by legal category of document, which is a different approach? Having heard what you yourself have said, that this dossier was given as a test, we wanted to test this possibility, and since there was evidence about what happened in all the villages, you chose Tulica as a particular village to suggest the way in which we could possibly proceed in order to abbreviate and narrow the issue, as they say in English, to focus more the case and the evidence specific to a particular town or village. That is where we are. We are now doing a village test, as such, and we must draw certain categories. We are not here appreciating a particular piece of evidence. Would that suit you, if the Trial Chamber examines different categories of documents and rules on them, how they can be admitted and under which conditions? What you have said about the civil law, the countries of the civil law system, is not quite correct because we are not here in the stage of investigation. We are in the trial stage, and we mustn't forget that, that we are already well into the trial now. A last point that I wish to address to you is that this does not prevent us from examining this dossier, nor does it prevent your office to avoid evidence which is repetitive. My colleague, Richard May, has already told you, I think, regarding Kaonik last week, when things have already been proven, we accept the competence given to us by the Rules, and we will reject the evidence that is repetitious of something that we have already heard. This is useless repetition, and all this in the interest of a fair, effective, and speedy process. Without entering into the details, this examination of the dossier by categories, would that suit you? That is the way I understood the question addressed to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Judge May's question, I think, said item by item, and I understood that to mean piece of evidence by piece of evidence rather than category by category. If I am wrong in that, I can deal with the proposition of category by category, but it would be our submission that item by item is far more helpful. Let me deal with that in two stages. Item by item is bound to be more helpful because what we are seeking to lay before you in the most efficient way is evidence that is not controversial. Evidence that is not controversial may come from a witness statement, it may come from a report, or it may come from another document, and, therefore, simply to deal with it on a category of material basis is possibly not appropriate. Why did we reduce the material to a dossier in the form of a statement or summary by the investigator? For the same reason. The material overall will reduce to a narrative account some paragraphs of which may be, some of which may not be genuinely in dispute. Thus, in our respectful submission, the appropriate approach of the Chamber could be to look at the individual propositions, factual propositions, and then to say, "Well, that is not shown as requiring any further examination. It's plainly not in dispute. No showing of dispute has been shown, and since that is supported by a witness statement or since that is supported by a report of a different kind, we will admit that piece of evidence," given that there is no bar imposed or implied on any particular category of evidence by your Rules. We would respectfully invite you to deal with it item by item. If it comes to category by category, it would be our position that the only way you can deal with it category by category is by saying that, in theory, everything is admissible because there is no block on the type of material you may consider and weigh, and so that you would have not got any further, or you may have got further, because you might, say, "We'll let all the maps in and we'll let the reports in, but we won't let any statements in," but this application and this approach by the Defence is all about statements. As I said right at the beginning of my reply, however disguised, this is a common law argument about hearsay, and, in a sense, it's inappropriate that such a blocking technique should be sought, really, by the Defence, but if not inappropriate -- perhaps "inappropriate" is the wrong word. I can't stand in the way of their conducting the case in the way that they choose, if they think it's in the interests of their defendant to do so. But we would invite you, therefore, to approach each piece of evidence or each summarised piece of evidence and extract and decide whether it's material that you can take into account at present on the basis of the material available or not. If not, then the evidence will be called. As to the repetition, I haven't yet myself analysed further how much Kaonik material you've had, and I'll deal with that because Judge May asked me to, and, of course, I will, but I suspect that there may be a little more of a problem with Kaonik than at first sight appears because of the need to prove the origin of particular individuals who are going to Kaonik for particular counts, but I'll come back to that. As to the general proposition that a Trial Chamber can say "Enough's enough," of course, it can. The Rules give you that power, and we recognise that. There is, of course, a potential problem, and that is that if a Prosecutor is cut off, "Well, you've had one witness on that topic, and that's enough," and the Defence then call contrary evidence at a later stage, the Trial Chamber may be embarrassed by having indicated satisfaction at an early stage when, on reflection, it finds it cannot be satisfied because of the Defence evidence that may be put on, and the Prosecutor may also be in the embarrassing position of then having to seek by rebuttal to add further to the evidence, but it only can do that if it knows what the Trial Chamber's later decision is, so there are problems there. All of those problems, in the standard adversarial system, are dealt with by the Prosecutor making his decision as to how many bits of evidence he wants to put in this scale on one side to ensure that however much the other side puts other evidence on the other scale, the scale stays down on the ground. I'm the first to recognise that we may need to be more flexible than that here in the interests of economy of time, but there are obvious difficulties with that, and I think they were difficulties that arose in the original case of Tadic, where there was an indication that something was satisfactorily dealt with by evidence, and then some counter-evidence emerged to outweigh it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Rules do allow for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Because they allow rebuttal evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you're not, as it were, stopped. You're not stopped from calling other evidence by the close of your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I make it plain, I have no desire, as I've made it plain throughout, I have no desire to repeat evidence where something has been given and hasn't been challenged, because it will be my argument in due course that that evidence must be acceptable and sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider these matters. Without reflecting, of course, on our decision, which we will have to give in due course, I'm grateful to the assistance that we've received in these arguments and on those who prepared all the material for us to consider. We will sit again at half past, and I hope we will have some evidence then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the witness is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we have, first of all, the witness's expert report, which we've read. We have also your overview. Now, I understand you want to ask some questions of the witness. In those circumstances, they could be fairly short, I would hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, and what I was proposing to do was to get the witness to go through, very quickly, the maps which in colour are rather better than they are in black and white, in that way to set out the history, and to ask him for a couple of the conclusions most material, and that would be about it. Incidentally, I should say sitting on the bench or counsels' row is Mr. Tomljanovich from the OTP, with your leave today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What I propose to do, again with your leave, is, first of all, to get the witness to give his full name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Robert J. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report, which the Chamber has read, you set out, at page 2, your personal history, which reveals how you studied, took your PhD. In the '70s and early '80s, you were a teacher. You then worked for Merrill Lynch, I think, in unrelated work but keeping a private interest in the area until retirement from that firm; meanwhile, in 1994 with John Fine, writing a book entitled "Bosnia and Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You set out, in an appendix, your curriculum vitae in more detail, and I only desire to ask you two or three questions to supplement that. First, I think you became a speaker of the language at the time that you were studying in the 1970s and early '80s.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although it may have gone rusty, you were able to revive it when you revived your interest in the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: In the 1990s, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your research, in the 1970s and '80s, did that include visits to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it did. I spent a year in several areas of the former Yugoslavia in 1974, '75, principally in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since your revived interest, what has been the approximate frequency of your visits? It says here "two or three trips a year," but is that about it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Since 1994, I've made two to three trips a year to the region for periods ranging from ten days to, more recently, six weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to visiting the area, do you maintain contact with other academics in the area when you're there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may be, and you'll have to tell us or you may tell us when you're asked other questions, but it may be that academics divide along lines sometimes holding extreme views in one direction or another. Are you acquainted, first of all, with the works of those who hold views that differ from yours?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: I try to be, yes, and the one safe prediction is that they will differ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You manage, so far as you can, to keep abreast of their publications and everything?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The opinions which I seek from you relate to just a few topics. You know what they are. First, there's the question of whether there was tribal hatred. Second, there's the boundaries of the constituent parts of the former Yugoslavia and claims for the legitimacy of those boundaries. Third, there's what was done in the 1990s, particularly in relation to arguments about boundaries, and, fourth, there's the question of international armed conflict. Is it your view that in relation to those topics upon which you hold an opinion, your knowledge of the history plays a part and perhaps an important part?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The history is set out in some detail as a resource for readers in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, the maps show the position quite well, and I would ask you now, please, to have in front of you, or to use the ELMO if the usher would turn it on, those maps, and we'll run through them very quickly as a guide for the Chamber. I've had them all put together in little clips, they have separate exhibit numbers, but I think that they may prove to be a useful and quick tool. So if we start with Z1685, this shows what, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: This is a map from an atlas of East European history, showing the hypotheses of various scholars regarding the origins of Slavic migrations in the 6th, 7th, and 8th centuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the continuous red line, the dotted red line, and the other interrupted red line, being the these theses of different academics?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But however different the theses may be, the marks of migration are broadly similar; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: There is general agreement that there was migration either in one, two, or more waves of Slavic speakers from one of these outlined areas to the area that I'm defining here to the north and east of the Adriatic Sea in the centuries that we've discussed. The map shows that there is very little scholarly agreement on the precise location of origin, and indeed there is further disagreement about the specific routes of migration and the number of waves of migration. But in general, this establishes the original homeland of the south Slavs and the possible routes that they took to areas that they've inhabited ever since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described it in your paper, I think, as being sedentary, in the sense that once they had arrived, they stayed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Unlike other migratory peoples who came and went, they indeed settled in this region, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next map, please, Z1687. You make the point in your paper that over the intervening centuries, the constituent parts of what was the former Yugoslavia had historically had greater and then smaller tracts of land to call their own, as it were?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: The political situation that developed in the centuries after the Slavic migrations led to the formation of several medieval empires or kingdoms. The first of these to arise was the Croatian kingdom in the 9th century.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the map we have here, the area coloured pink?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: This map is really a map of the Croatian kingdom at its presumed farthest domains, that is, in that area which it may well have ruled or covered in the period of approximately 925 to 930.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next map, please, Z1648.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Following the collapse of the Croatian kingdom, there arose a Serbian medieval empire, and this map shows the presumed farthest extent of the rule of the Serbian empire. Just to orient within the space that we are speaking about, the Drina River, that is, the contemporary eastern boundary of Bosnia, runs right here, so this map shows that at one time virtually all of Herzegovina was a part of the Serbian empire, and parts of Bosnia as well were a part of the medieval Serbian empire in the time frame indicated on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this map for Serbia a map showing as large an area of land that had ever been titled "Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. There were small areas that were briefly also under Serbian rule, but this indicates, I think, its farthest extent for most purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next map, please, 1666.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: This is a map of the medieval Bosnian kingdom, which began as a State in a small area indicated by the dotted line here (indicating). Unlike the Serbian and Croatian States, Bosnia had inland origins and developed around a small island of land that had no coastal outlet originally. The date for this inner area is approximately 1180. I have my pointer right here just below the city of Bugojno (indicating) to provide perhaps some orientation on the map. This again is the River Drina (indicating), which is present-day Bosnia's eastern boundary. The Bosnian State extended in the next two centuries, and under Stepan Kotromanic, reached approximately these boundaries by about 1326. It finally, at the greatest extent of its control in about 1377, reached the outer boundaries to include virtually all of the northern Adriatic coast and, indeed, significant portions of Serbia, and this was the situation when the king was crowned in 1377 as both king of Bosnia and of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn over, please, to the next two maps. First, 1651, which shows the Balkan Peninsula, 1817 to 1877, and with that in mind also turn over to the next map, Z1652, where Bosnia-Herzegovina is shown perhaps in a triangular shape we more immediately recognise.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Let me suggest we put 652 underneath and perhaps put 651 right on top of it. The reason for selecting these maps for illustration purposes is that with the advance of the Ottoman Empire into this part of the Balkans, indeed Ottoman control extended over much of those territories that were governed by the three medieval empires that we just identified. In the process, the area of Bosnia takes, for the first time, something which looks like its present-day contour. This would be a map from relatively late in the Ottoman administration, but the administrative units that made up Bosnia were, indeed, in place within about a century or virtually all in place within a century of the initial Ottoman presence. In 1878, the European powers at the Congress of Berlin awarded Bosnia and Herzegovina to Austria-Hungary to administer, and at that point Austro-Hungarian rule took over using essentially the same boundaries, very few changes, that existed in the last years of Ottoman rule. The familiar triangular shape of Bosnia-Herzegovina is very identifiable in this map as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, in fact, for how long had that shape of Bosnia-Herzegovina existed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
