utterances.text: By the late 19th century, we can say that the shape of Bosnia and Herzegovina existed for several centuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not shown certainly as to its eastern boundary on the map 1651?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what do you say about the reality of its eastern boundary, then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Well, the reality of its eastern boundary, it became an administrative reality early in the Ottoman period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So with the familiar shape on Z1652, can we go to the next map, 1662, which has been marked in hand as "1918"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: This is a map of the constituent parts that came together to form the kingdom of the Serb, Croats and Slovenes in 1918, and again the very familiar shape of Bosnia as a triangular entity, Bosnia-Herzegovina, is recognisable. In fact, the Bosnia and Herzegovina entity was recognised as distinctive in the constitution of that kingdom, which was voted into effect in 1921, and remained an administered entity until 1924. Then its boundaries continued to be exacted the same as they were earlier until 1929.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next map, please. The word "banovina" features in some of the evidence that we've heard. I think it's right that there are two events in the 20th century in particular where the word "banovina" may crop up in identifying relevant boundaries, and this map, Z1654, from 1929, is the first, and it may be a less relevant place where "banovina" has some significance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: The word "banovina" derives its name from a territory -- or means a territory of a Ban, which was the word used for medieval rulers of Bosnia and certainly in Croatia, and therefore refers to a territory governed by a governor. In 1929, upset with the restive nature of nationality relations in the kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, the king promulgated a -- he suspended the constitution and redrew the internal boundaries of the kingdom in such a way that they totally ignored nationality divisions and historical divisions and simply adopted natural features as guidelines. These are the banovinas, then, of the 1929 act and prevailed as administrative units until 1939. Thus, for the first time for many centuries, Bosnia and Herzegovina lost its distinctive shape and its boundaries were disregarded in internal boundary formation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And nationalities were not respected in the transection of nationality boundaries?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: That is correct, except in the case of the Slovenes to the north, who really did receive some respect for their national homeland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next map, please, 1665.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to cut you short for a second, this is the second place where the word "banovina" is likely to feature in people dealing with comparatively recent history, probably the more significant use. Can you explain this to us, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. In 1939, another internal redefinition of boundaries took place after protracted negotiations between the Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, Cvetkovic, and the leader of the Croatian Peasant Party, Vlatko Macek, so this boundary solution which prevailed from August of 1939 until April of 1941 goes by the somewhat unmanageable name of the Cvetkovic-Macek Agreement and is frequently referred to, for shorthand, as the Banovina Plan or simply as the Sporazum, which means "agreement."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just mark out, please, with a marker, the area of the banovina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: (Witness complies)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that area greater or smaller than present-day Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: That is substantially greater than present-day Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at the area to the bottom right-hand part of that banovina, we see Travnik, Bugojno, and was the Lasva Valley and Central Bosnia incorporated within the banovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: In fact, the Lasva Valley was a part of the Croatian banovina, and the boundary ran right through it. So the area that is generally being discussed in this proceeding was, in fact, a part of but right on the boundary of the Croatian banovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This area of Croatian land, as it then was, is smaller than that medieval map which encompassed much more. But that apart, is this the largest amount of land that has ever been in Croatian control?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Well, no. World War II gave the Croatian state more, but I think the importance of this configuration was that it has become a source of nostalgia and, indeed, a kind of a minimalist programme for expansion for Croatian nationalists ever since the banovina plan was abandoned in 1941 and, certainly, in the period after 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although, of course, like the present shape of Croatia, although to a different degree, it has, as it were, a hole, in the middle, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it does. The large area which is, indeed, a substantial part of Bosnia-Herzegovina was left as part of the remainder of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next map, please, 1657. This deals, indeed, with wartime Croatia, 1941, the yellow, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: The 1941 attack on Yugoslavia by Germany resulted in a divided occupation of the lands of Yugoslavia indicated by this heavy black line running right down the centre of the country. To the north of that line was German occupied, to the south of it, southwest of it was Italian occupied. The large yellow area in the middle was the independent state of Croatia, in its local language abbreviation, the NDH, and included all of historical Bosnia-Herzegovina and much of the Croatian state that had existed on the eve of World War I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Run by whom?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: It was run by the Ustasha, which were a group of collaborators with the German and Italian occupiers who were considered and may be considered as extreme Croatian nationalists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next map, please, 1660.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: At the end of World War II --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is marked 1945, and tell us about this.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: This is the map of the republics, the socialist republics that made up the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. These boundaries were essentially drawn in 1945 and did not change until the early 1990s, and, in fact, the boundaries largely still exist as they are here, although in a different political form. The traditional, historical boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina are, indeed, reestablished with the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina one of six socialist republics making up federal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So subject to the interruption first by the ten-year banovina map and then the two-year banovina map and then the occupation, for how many years had this shape of Bosnia-Herzegovina been an identified country?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Well, it's almost 500 years. It's 500 years or, perhaps, a little bit more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now turn, please, to the other map, the separate map? No, the big one. This one the Chamber doesn't yet have -- I'm sorry. They do have it; I don't. It's a little big for the ELMO, but I think we can deal with it in segments. This is a map built on census information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: That's correct, the census of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To interpret the map, let's take any of the circular graphs, for example, the biggest one, Sarajevo, if you can just point to that. It's easiest for us all to see.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is shown there, as the key reveals, is the total population of that particular city broken down as to green for Muslims, a rather, in the photocopied form, muddy-brown/red colour, the right, for Serbs, and then blue for Croats, white for others, and then the other piece of the chart, 10.7, what's that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: That is the percentage of persons who declared themselves as Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at the map overall, obviously, we can simply look for colour to see where any particular group is most concentrated. In some places, green comes to the eye, in some places, blue, and so on, but what can you tell us about this map, from your point of view, that is of significance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: This map features the breakdown of the population of towns and cities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it shows that, with a very few exceptions, those towns and cities were truly mixed in population by national declaration, and the composition of Bosnia-Herzegovina was such that, again, with a few exceptions, boundary drawing between the nationalities is simply not a feasible exercise. Let me go over briefly the exceptions. First is an area to the west of the city of Mostar which shows here as almost exclusively blue, which is a virtually exclusively Croatian population in Western Herzegovina. To the far northwest is a nearly exclusively Muslim population, to the north and west of Bihac, and then finally, a relatively sparsely populated, almost exclusively Serbian area here in the extreme western part of Bosnia. With the exception of these population concentrations, the picture is, indeed, thoroughly mixed for the towns and cities, and with respect to the rural areas, a similar pattern of very mixed population generally prevails, with the exceptions I've noted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Back to the clip of maps, we can take the large one off the ELMO, please. The next map, please, Z1675.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: This is a map which indicates, by outline, the municipalities included in the declarations, the self-declarations of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which was November 18th, 1991, and of the Posavina, an area that borders Croatia in the northern part of Bosnia, which was just one week earlier in November of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last map, Z6709, perhaps a little out of time to deal with it because I may deal with it by questions a little later, but nevertheless let's deal with it now as a map, the Vance-Owen Plan at the top, the 2nd of January, 1993, and the Serb proposal for union of the three republics in June of 1993. Comments, please, as to, first, the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: The top map of January 1993 shows the proposed establishment of provinces under the Vance-Owen Plan as first made public in January of 1993. It shows that while there is substantial convergence between the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, it, indeed, gives a very generous proportion of territory to the Croatian-dominated provinces, first of all, relative to the population distribution and, second, relative to subsequent international proposals. The bottom map is a map that was proposed after the top one was rejected by the Serbian side in April and May of 1993 and shows that the Posavina area here is substantially cut down and, indeed, that there is a deep protrusion into the Croatian territories that were awarded in the earlier map in the area north of Mostar and in the Central Bosnia region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. A couple of topics related to that geographical history. First, the arrival of Muslims in this area at all, can you just explain that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: The Muslims did not actually arrive. They were converts to Islam from the indigenous Slavic population in the period immediately prior to and during the first 140 years of the Ottoman rule, so roughly from 1460 or so through about the year 1600. It will be remembered that this was a period of substantial religious change throughout Europe, in fact, it coincides with the reformation, but the conversions to Islam in Bosnia took place not in response to any massive effort at forced conversions by the Ottoman rule but rather through conversions on village by village, individual by individual, over an extended period of time and from various sources. Many of the converts to Islam were Catholic before, some were members of the medieval Bosnian church, and a few came from yet other groups. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you said that some of this actually happened prior to the Ottoman arrival. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When did that come about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: It was very limited in terms of what we know, but, indeed, as we sit here, the authorities in Sarajevo are excavating a tekija that existed prior to the Ottoman conquest of Bosnia. So we know there was some Islamic presence in the very few years just prior to the Ottoman conquest of the area. It presumably was quite limited and may very well have been only a rural or urban phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I should like to address a question to the expert, Mr. Nice. Professor Donia, you said, regarding the conversion to Islam around the middle of the 15th century, you told us a moment ago reading the maps that Bosnia existed as an entity since the 14th century. What is the distinction between Bosnia as an entity that you showed us on the map since the 14th century and this Islamisation or conversion to Islam? Are they the same Bosniaks or does that have nothing to do with what we saw in the previous entry in the Middle Ages on the maps?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: There were no conversions to Islam during the period of the medieval Bosnian state, except for perhaps the very last few years of its existence. So the medieval Bosnian state existed independent of and prior to the conversions to Islam that took place starting at about 1460.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I have another question for you, Professor Donia. You said it was the conversion of Slavs to the Islamic faith. What is the distinction between what you call the Bosniak state? We can't even talk about a state because the state came into being much later. So a Bosnian entity, what distinguished it in the 14th century?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: The Bosnian state, what I've referred to as the medieval Bosnian kingdom, existed with a king from 1377 until 1391 and ultimately fell to Ottoman domination. The term "Bosnian" refers to the inhabitants of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which, as you've just indicated, exists as an entity for many centuries, but as a state, only in this period of the medieval era and then in the immediate years of our present decade. The term "Bosniak," which is used now since 1993 by the members of the group that used to be known as the Bosnian Muslims, refers to a nationality and should be distinguished from the residents of the territory of the state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just picking up on Judge Bennouna's questions and your answers to them, the territory that was the medieval Bosnian kingdom, did that remain an identified unit, not withstanding its domination by others, or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: The shape of the medieval Bosnian kingdom at its farthest extent included, perhaps we'll recall the entire northern Dalmatian coast, so when the Ottoman administration began and the area was conquered by the Ottomans and also partly by Venice, that is when Bosnia first assumed its presently identifiable shape, that is, Bosnia lost its coastal territories and became an inland state with its familiar triangular shape in the first century of Ottoman rule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And retained those boundaries, broadly speaking, thereafter?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: And retained those boundaries, broadly speaking, under Ottoman, Austro-Hungarian, Yugoslav, royal Yugoslav, and subsequent socialist Yugoslav rule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that identity of territory being or not being built on religion in any way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: It was not, per se, built on religion or religious identification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps that can conveniently lead me to a next topic upon which I want your assistance. It is said sometimes that what happened in the 1990s reflected ancient tribal hatreds in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your comment, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: The notion of ancient tribal hatreds, that is, that people in this region have been killing each other by nationality or religion for many centuries really first entered the region as a distinct belief in the early 1990s. It was advocated by diplomats and leaders of western countries who wanted to characterise the conflict in such a way that they could justify inaction or lack of policy initiatives to end the conflict. It was also adopted by many journalists and writers who wanted to paint this conflict as exotic, Oriental, interesting, and one in which wild, savage people were killing one another. I find no basis for this belief in the national views or the intellectual views, really, of any of the south Slav nationalities. It was a western imposition of the early 1990s. I find little to justify this view in the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am not arguing that there was not conflict, contention, and violence, but that violence was not, until the 20th century, national or ethnic, nor religious in the main. It was frequently social between peasants and landlords or between outside countries, particularly in the Middle Ages, seeking to invade, conquer small parts or all of Bosnia. So violence, there was, contention, there was, but I find nothing to say that there was tribal conflict after sometime in the Middle Ages when tribes essentially disappeared from the scene and only occasional limited instances of national, ethnic, or religious conflict of a violent form through the centuries up until the late 19th century.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout those centuries, how many different religions were represented in the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Well, many. The four primary ones were Catholicism, Orthodoxy, Islam, and Judaism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next topic, which we can deal with shortly, with your very abbreviated summary of the history, at the time of the conflict in the early 1990s, what reliance, if any, was placed on that history by leaders such as President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: I'd like to make the analogy to the old man staring in the mirror and seeing in the reflection a very young person. I think that the entire conflict represented, in many ways, a revival or invention of historical understanding based on previous events that were, in many cases, fabricated or greatly misleading. But the use of the medieval empires to form nationalist claims, the use of religious influences to advance cultural claims, the use of the banovina plan of 1939 to advance territorial claims, and even the use of vocabulary, with the Croats and Muslims developing a pejorative term for the Serbs who were actively fighting them which was Chetniks, or those Croats who were actively fighting which became Ustasha, these all had historical origins, as did the references to Bosnian Muslims as Turks, which, of course, they are not and were not but nevertheless was a pejorative term derived from historical understanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And President Tudjman, in particular?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: President Tudjman, in particular, developed the view, when writing as a historian in the 1970s, that Bosnia, in whole, belonged to Croatia. He specifically argued that Bosnia was part of the economic and geopolitical essence, if you will, of Croatia and developed the view that the Bosnian Muslims were essentially Croats. He is frequently quoted as saying that 80 per cent of the Muslims were Croats. Now, on that basis, he derives the argument then that the Croats enjoy a demographic majority in Bosnia, which would be true if, indeed, the Muslims were Croats. He further, in the course of the pragmatic events of the early 1990s, adopted a somewhat more pragmatic fallback position which was to advocate the development of a Croatia that extended to the old banovina line of 1939.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the second of the banovinas, the one that is the same shape as present Croatia but with more territory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as leaders of the Croat community in Bosnia-Herzegovina itself is concerned, what was their interaction with President Tudjman on the evidence available?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: There was a great deal of interaction between President Tudjman and the Croatian leadership in Bosnia-Herzegovina, if not daily, one could say at least very regularly. Many of the Croatian leadership in Bosnia essentially broke down into two viewpoints, one which was that Bosnia-Herzegovina represented a state, an entity in which the national aspirations of all Croats could be realised. A small group developed the view that that could take place only within a distinct territorial unit, and it was with that group that President Tudjman had the greatest contact and developed the strongest support. He sponsored them, in many instances, gave them specific directives and broad programmes to implement and agendas to carry out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Karadjordjevo, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: In March of 1991, President Tudjman and President Milosevic of Serbia met in the Karadjordjevo, the former hunting lodge of the royal family, and reportedly discussed the partition of Bosnia. This meeting is now the subject of many hundreds of articles and discussions, but on the basis of participants at the meeting, I think we can say now that there was an agreement in principle between the two of them to pursue the division of Bosnia but no agreement on specifically where that dividing line would be. In fact, a commission was established to draw those lines but never was able to reach an agreement. From that point on, one can clearly trace the line through the behaviour of the Croat leadership that supported division in response to President Tudjman's initiatives, and that represents the point really from which the Croatian agenda for division of Bosnia with the eye towards ultimate annexation to Croatia emerges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the absence of annexation, when the Vance-Owen Plan was proposed, we needn't look at it again, but you distinguished it from the later plan of June 1993 which had less territory going to Croatia, when the Vance-Owen Plan was advanced, what was the perhaps understandable reaction of the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Mr. Mate Boban signed it as soon as he could find a pen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A word on the June 1991 meetings, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: In June of 1991, which is about three months after the Karadjordjevo meeting, President Tudjman held two meetings with the leaders of the various municipalities of areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina in which Croats had a substantial demographic presence. The first of these was on June 13th, 1991, and the second was on June 20th, 1991. In those meetings, there was a great deal of discussion, as reported subsequently in the press, of the various approaches to Bosnia and Herzegovina, but the directive that represented the outcome of those meetings was to establish, over time, a separate Croatian community in Bosnia and Herzegovina which would tend towards separation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was present on behalf of the Croatians, do you know, at those meetings in June or -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: Well, there were two meetings. One was for the Herzegovinan Croats and one for the Bosnian Croats, and Mr. Dario Kordic was reported being at the second meeting and as having taken a leadership role in the discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the war, the influence of Croatia, if at all, on what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: The leadership of the Croatian state, by which I mean President Tudjman and his regime, played a leading role throughout the war, frequently negotiated on behalf of the Bosnian and Herzegovinan Croats, literally spoke on their behalf and advocated their position. In addition, there was substantial military arms, actual troop support, and financing of the troops of the Bosnian Croat forces. In fact, to this day, the Croat forces in Bosnia receive part of their income directly from Croatia. So both on the military front and on the political front, the Croatian state was exercising leadership and direction for the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give me some examples of negotiations by President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: President Tudjman, first of all, met, at first instance, clearly at Karadjordjevo with this meeting with President Milosevic in March of 1991. On the first 15 days of January in 1992, he met directly with the member of the presidency of the Serbs of Bosnia, Nikola Koljevic, in Zagreb and was informed of the Serbian plans to proclaim a separate republic, which took place right about that time. Subsequently, he negotiated with Lord Owen and Mr. Vance, he negotiated with various other people in the International Community, and in particular had a very interesting meeting with U.S. Ambassador Warren Zimmerman on January 14th, 1992, in which he tried for an hour to convince him that Bosnia should belong to Croatia. Finally, even in the disillusion of Herceg-Bosna, which was mandated by the Dayton Agreements, President Tudjman met with President Clinton of the United States on April 2, 1996, and after that meeting pledged that Herceg-Bosna would be dissolved. It subsequently was dissolved or to the satisfaction of the International Community, in any case, later that fall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You adopt your report as the balance of your evidence in chief, I think.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA
utterances.text: I would be glad to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examination tomorrow. How long do you anticipate, Mr. Stein?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I expect I'll be Tuesday and, with the Court's permission, Wednesday, and we'll see how we go from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll start with Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Always a good beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not so sure about Wednesday. Dr. Donia, could you be back, please, tomorrow afternoon at half past two, and we'll go on with your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a rule here that witnesses, once they've begun their evidence, should not speak to anybody about their evidence, and that includes the Prosecution. So would you remember that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Half past two tomorrow then.
